site_article.headline: What is Granola AI and how to use it for meeting notes
site_article.dek: Granola is a desktop notepad that listens to your calls without a bot, then turns your rough notes and the transcript into a clean summary. Here is how to set it up, what the free plan leaves out, and where it falls short.
site_article.summary: Granola is an AI notepad that captures your computer's audio during meetings, so no bot joins the call, and combines your own notes with the transcript afterward. The free Basic plan keeps 30 days of history, and Business costs $14 per user per month.
site_article.seo_title: What is Granola AI and how to use it for meeting notes
site_article.seo_description: What is Granola AI: how the bot-free meeting notepad works, how to set it up, use templates and Granola Chat, what the free plan limits, and how to tell people.
site_article.answer_summary: Granola is an AI meeting notepad for Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android. It transcribes your computer's audio without adding a bot to the call, then expands the notes you typed into a full summary you can edit and search.
site_article.hero_alt: A Granola notes window next to a video call with six people on screen.

paragraphs.text: What is Granola AI, in short: a notepad for meetings. You open a note when a call starts, type whatever you would normally jot down, and Granola transcribes the conversation in the background. When the call ends, it rewrites your rough notes into a full summary using the transcript. The company describes it as an AI notepad for people with back-to-back meetings, and it works without a meeting bot.

That last part is the main reason people pick it. Most AI notetakers join your Zoom or Teams call as an extra participant. Granola's desktop app on macOS and Windows captures the audio on your computer directly, so nobody sees a bot in the participant list. There are also apps for iPhone and Android, and a web app at notes.granola.ai that can view and edit notes but cannot transcribe.
How to set up Granola

paragraphs.title: 1. Install the desktop app
paragraphs.text: Download Granola from its website. On a Mac, open the downloaded file and drag Granola into your Applications folder. On Windows, run the installer. The Mac app needs macOS 14 or later.

paragraphs.title: 2. Sign in with Google or Microsoft
paragraphs.text: Click Sign in and finish in your browser. Granola only supports Google and Microsoft sign-in. Use your work account if you have one, because Granola builds your meeting list from that calendar. When it asks for calendar permissions, choose Select all, then Continue.

paragraphs.title: 3. Allow audio access
paragraphs.text: On a Mac, click Allow on the microphone and system audio prompts. Windows grants both automatically. You can review them later in your system's Privacy and Security settings.

paragraphs.title: 4. Watch the demo meeting
paragraphs.text: After the first sign-in, Granola opens a short demo meeting that shows the whole flow in about two minutes. After that, your home screen lists upcoming meetings from your calendar.
How to take meeting notes with Granola

paragraphs.title: 5. Start a note when the call starts
paragraphs.text: Click the meeting notification, open the meeting from your home screen, or click New Note for a call that is not on your calendar. Granola does not transcribe in the background on its own: a meeting is only transcribed when you have a note open for it.

paragraphs.title: 6. Type a few cues, not everything
paragraphs.text: Write down only what matters to you: a decision, a number to check, a name. Granola uses those lines to decide what the summary should focus on. In the transcript, your microphone shows up as Me and the other side as Them, unless speaker names are available.

paragraphs.title: 7. Stop the transcript yourself
paragraphs.text: Granola stops when it detects the call has ended, after 15 minutes of silence, or when your computer sleeps. Do not count on that. If you have back-to-back calls, press stop between them, or two meetings can end up in one transcript.

paragraphs.title: 8. Pick a template
paragraphs.text: Templates set the structure of the finished notes. During a call, type a forward slash in your notes and choose one. After the notes are generated, click the dropdown arrow on the Enhanced tab and pick another template, and the notes are rewritten in that format. Templates only work in the desktop apps.

Make your own template for each meeting you repeat, such as a weekly team check-in or a sales call. Granola's docs suggest saying what you want from the meeting, how long the notes should be, and which sections to include, such as decisions and action items.
Ask Granola Chat about your meetings

Granola Chat sits at the bottom of the desktop and iPhone apps. Where you open it decides what it searches: one meeting, a folder, a set of meetings you select, or everything from the home screen. It only knows your meeting notes and files you add, not your email or to-do lists. On the free Basic plan, Chat covers the last 30 days of notes.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 1: Before a call
paragraphs.text: What did we decide in the last meeting with [client name], and what did we promise to send them?

paragraphs.title: Prompt 2: Right after a call
paragraphs.text: List every action item from this meeting as a table with the task, the person who owns it and the deadline if one was said. Mark anything that had no owner.

paragraphs.title: Prompt 3: Across many meetings
paragraphs.text: Which topics came up in more than one of these meetings? For each one, give the meetings where it came up and what was said.

If you ask the same thing after every call, save it as a Recipe. Type a forward slash in the chat bar, choose Create a recipe, give it a name and a prompt, and say whether it runs on single meetings or multiple meetings. Recipes run as written and do not support placeholders, so leave the brackets out.
What Granola costs

Granola lists three plans. Basic is free and keeps 30 days of meeting history; it leaves out integrations such as Notion and Zapier, pre-meeting briefs, follow-up emails and API access. Business costs $14 per user per month with unlimited history. Enterprise costs $35 per user per month and adds admin controls such as single sign-on and workspace-wide policies. If you drop from Business to Basic, older notes are hidden, not deleted.
Consent: tell people you are using it

No bot in the call also means nobody is told automatically. Granola's own guidance says participants should know when you use an AI notetaker, that recording laws differ by region, and that you should check with your legal or IT team. It also suggests pausing the transcript if a conversation turns sensitive.

paragraphs.title: 9. Turn on the transparency features
paragraphs.text: Go to Settings, then Preferences, then Transparency. The automated chat message posts a short notice in the meeting chat when you start transcribing. For Google Meet it needs the Granola browser extension. The Granola Watermark puts a small badge on your camera video while Granola is listening.
What Granola is bad at

Granola does not save audio or video, so there is nothing to play back when a line in the transcript looks wrong, and it cannot import recordings you already have. On desktop it captures all system audio at once, so music or other sounds on your computer can end up in the transcript. Speakers are often inferred from context, so names can be attributed to the wrong person. The phone apps cannot capture audio from video call apps.

Independent reviewers point to the same gaps. A review on the blog of tl;dv, a competitor, called the missing playback a real problem when a transcript in Russian came out poorly. Zack Proser, who uses Granola daily and links to it as an affiliate, recommends checking names, numbers and dates against the transcript for a few minutes after each meeting.

Granola fits people who sit in a lot of video calls, want to stay in the conversation instead of typing, and do not need a recording afterward. It fits less well if you need audio to prove what was said, or if your team has strict rules about where meeting data is processed. Try it on a few ordinary meetings on the free plan, turn on the chat message from day one, and read the first summaries closely before you trust them.
